props.title: Five Fingers of Death

sections.content: Five Fingers of Death ignited the international kung fu craze, becoming Warner Bros' first major martial arts release in America. The film's iconic "iron palm" technique, where Lo Lieh's hands glow red before delivering devastating blows, influenced everything from Kill Bill Vol. 2 (2004) to video games like Street Fighter. Its success opened the floodgates for Shaw Brothers classics in Western markets, arriving just months before Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon (1973) would revolutionize the genre globally.

movies.slug: Gordon Liu's masterpiece about a student becoming a kung fu master through intensive training chambers

sections.content: The film's tournament structure and training sequences created a blueprint that martial arts movies still follow today. Director Chung Chang-wha crafted intense fight choreography that emphasized the brutality of combat while maintaining the artistic elements of kung fu cinema. This balance influenced later works like The Last Dragon (1985) and Bloodsport (1988), which adapted these elements for Western audiences.

Beyond its action sequences, Five Fingers of Death established crucial genre elements like the revenge narrative, corrupt martial arts schools, and the student-master relationship. These themes echo through films like Iron Monkey (1993) and Ip Man (2008), showing how this early Shaw Brothers hit helped define martial arts storytelling conventions. sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond martial arts cinema. Its training montages and power-up sequences influenced Western action films like Rocky IV (1985) and even superhero movies like Doctor Strange (2016). The glowing hands technique became a visual shorthand for martial arts power, referenced in countless films and TV shows.
